newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chernomyrdin brushes up image as Yeltsin ails.
newsitem.headline: Chernomyrdin brushes up image as Yeltsin ails.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin made a striking television appearance on Monday, playing the accordion, sharing his favourite recipe and looking for all the world like a president-in-waiting.
As Boris Yeltsin entered the final stages of preparation for open heart surgery, the man who will take over the Kremlin while he is under the knife was busy cultivating the human touch.

The 58-year-old Chernomyrdin, hitherto known by most Russians as a dour bureaucrat, was shown on a jet-ski and dangling his grandson on his knee. He admitted to liking vodka and said he regretted not having more time for beautiful women.
The programme on NTV commercial television was called The Unknown Chernomyrdin. It opened with the prime minister, who has a limousine with police escort at his disposal, driving his own modest car.

Wearing a grey cap and windbreaker, he even checked the oil when he arrived at his weekend residence in the government complex of Barvikha outside Moscow, where Yeltsin is resting ahead of his planned bypass operation.
The Kremlin leader, who dropped out of sight just before he won an election to a second term in July, has handed over some of his powers to Chernomyrdin during to his illness.

But Yeltsin's absence has prompted a lively power struggle in the Kremlin and several potential successors are polishing up their images. The television said the programme was part of a series and that communist leader Gennady Zyuganov would be next.

Sitting by the kitchen table with his wife, his grandson Andrei on his lap, and a traditional Russian glass of tea in front of him, Chernomrydin laughed modestly when asked who was the head of the family. "I suppose I am," he said.

But when the interview moved to his office Chernomyrdin showed a more forceful side, hinting at the Kremlin intrigue which has increased since Yeltsin announced on September 5 that doctors had recommended heart surgery.

Asked whether politicians could be friends, he said: "There can be no friends in politics, there can only be comrades-in-arms. In politics you have to act tough sometimes. I am used to relying on people, I cannot stand deceit. I cannot stand lies, and I do not forgive them."
Chernomyrdin who became chairman of the board of the huge state gas concern Gazprom in 1989, said he had never sought popularity and had not wanted to become prime minister in 1992.
"But Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) just said: "You must.' I saw what was going on. I saw it myself."

Back in the kitchen his wife Valentina gushed about their courtship, before her husband began losing his hair. "He was a village lad, tall and never skinny like those city guys. He had a great quiff, not like now. He was very handsome," she said.
Chernomyrdin showed off his musical talent, playing a Russian folk song on the accordion for his female interviewer, who asked him if he had time to notice beautiful women.
"Yes, I have time, but only to notice, and nothing more. Which I regret deeply," he said.
He said he liked reading Boris Pasternak, Alexander Solzenitzin, Ivan Turgenev and Russian philosophy and shared his recipe for potato dumplings.
He also admitted to a taste for vodka, but in strictly limited quantities. "Just a bit, a bit yes...but the main thing is not to overdo it. Never."
The interview focused on his health, showing Russians that a vigorous man was at the helm in the captain's absence, and even provided a glimpse of his failings.
Chernomyrdin, whose speech tends to ramble, said he had got letters from the public offering coaching. "I know it's a problem," he said. "I wish I had more time."
